questions.stem: In which year is the Western Roman Empire traditionally said to have ended, when its last emperor was overthrown?
options: 410 CE
27 BCE
476 CE
questions.explanation: In 476 CE the Germanic leader Odoacer removed the boy emperor Romulus Augustulus, and no new emperor was named in the west. In 410 the Visigoths sacked Rome, a huge shock, but emperors kept ruling in the west for decades afterwards. The year 1453 is when Constantinople fell, ending the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire.

questions.stem: In the feudal system, what was a fief?
options: A tax of one-tenth of every harvest, paid to the local Church
A written promise from the king to limit his own powers
A wooden tower built on top of a raised mound of earth
Land granted by a lord in return for loyalty and service
questions.explanation: A fief was land (and the income from it) that a lord granted to a vassal, who in return promised loyalty and service, usually as a mounted knight. The tenth of a harvest paid to the Church was a tithe, a separate payment that every Christian owed.

questions.stem: Which group made up the great majority of people in medieval Europe?
options: Knights who served their lords as heavily armed mounted soldiers
Clergy such as priests, monks, nuns and bishops
Nobles who held large estates granted by the king
Peasants, including serfs who were bound to the land
questions.explanation: Most medieval people — around nine in ten — were peasants who farmed the land, and many of them were serfs tied to a lord's manor. Knights, clergy and nobles were small groups at the top of the hierarchy, even though they appear most often in written records.

questions.stem: A knight kneels before a lord, places his hands between the lord's hands and swears to be loyal. What is taking place?
options: A trial by ordeal before a village priest
A guild ceremony admitting a new master
An act of homage and an oath of fealty
A sentence of excommunication by a bishop
questions.explanation: Homage was the ceremony in which a vassal became the lord's man, and the oath of fealty was his sworn promise of loyalty; in return the lord gave protection and often a fief. Excommunication was a Church punishment that cut a person off from the sacraments, the opposite of being welcomed into a relationship.

questions.stem: How did a serf differ from a free peasant?
options: A serf owned the land they farmed outright and owed the lord nothing
A serf served as a mounted soldier in the lord's own army
A serf could not leave the manor without the lord's permission
A serf was paid wages in coins for every day of work done
questions.explanation: Serfs were unfree: they were bound to the manor, owed labour on the lord's land and needed his permission to leave or even to marry. Serfs were not paid wages for that labour — they worked the lord's land as a duty in return for strips of land to farm for themselves.

questions.stem: What was a tithe?
options: A yearly fee paid to a guild by every craftsman in the town
A fine paid to a lord for grinding grain at the lord's mill
A tenth of a person's produce or income, given to the Church
A tenth of a knight's land, handed back to the king each year
questions.explanation: Christians were expected to give the Church a tithe — one-tenth of their crops, animals or income — which supported priests, churches and monasteries. Paying the lord to use his mill was a separate feudal charge, owed to the lord rather than the Church.

questions.stem: What did it mean when the pope excommunicated someone?
options: They were raised to the rank of bishop or abbot
They were burned at the stake as a convicted heretic
They were shut out of the Church and its sacraments
They were declared a saint of the Church after death
questions.explanation: Excommunication cut a person off from the Church's sacraments, which medieval people believed put their soul in danger of hell; for a king it could also turn his subjects and allies against him. Burning was a punishment for heresy carried out by secular rulers, not what excommunication itself meant.

questions.stem: Why were monasteries important to learning in the early Middle Ages?
options: Monks printed thousands of cheap books on presses in their own workshops
Monks ran free schools that taught every peasant child to read
Monks destroyed ancient Greek and Roman books as pagan works
Monks copied by hand and preserved books, including ancient texts
questions.explanation: In scriptoriums, monks copied books by hand — the Bible, but also many Latin works from ancient Rome — and so preserved knowledge that might otherwise have been lost. Printing presses did not reach Europe until about 1450, so for most of the Middle Ages every book was handwritten.

questions.stem: What was an illuminated manuscript?
options: A handwritten book decorated with bright colours and gold
A printed book produced on a Gutenberg-style printing press
A carved stone panel set above a cathedral's main doorway
A royal charter fixed with the king's large wax seal
questions.explanation: Illuminated manuscripts were handwritten books, usually made by monks, decorated with coloured pictures, patterned borders and gold or silver leaf that seemed to light up the page. They were made long before printing, which is why each one is unique.

questions.stem: Why did castle builders move from motte-and-bailey castles to stone castles?
options: The pope ordered that all timber castles had to be pulled down
Stone castles needed no soldiers inside to defend them
Stone was much harder to burn or break down than timber
Stone castles were quicker and cheaper to build than timber
questions.explanation: The first Norman motte-and-bailey castles were wooden towers on earth mounds, quick to build but easy to set alight. Stone keeps and walls resisted fire and siege weapons far better, although they cost much more and took years to build.

questions.stem: In which year did William of Normandy defeat King Harold at the Battle of Hastings?
questions.explanation: William of Normandy defeated and killed Harold Godwinson at Hastings in 1066 and was crowned King of England that Christmas. The year 1215 is Magna Carta, 1095 is the call for the First Crusade and 1348 is when the Black Death reached England.

questions.stem: What was the Domesday Book, ordered by William the Conqueror in 1085?
options: A list of the crimes and punishments used in every shire
A survey recording who held land in England and what it was worth
A law code that limited the king's power over his barons
A long embroidered cloth telling the whole story of the Norman Conquest
questions.explanation: Domesday was a huge survey of England's land, people, animals and property, so the king knew what each place was worth and how much tax it could pay. The embroidered cloth showing the conquest is the Bayeux Tapestry, a different source.

questions.stem: Magna Carta (1215) was significant mainly because it:
options: freed all serfs in England from service to their lords
abolished the English monarchy and created a republic
established the idea that the king must obey the law too
gave every adult in England the right to vote for parliament
questions.explanation: King John was forced by rebel barons to agree to Magna Carta, which set out that even the king was bound by the law and could not punish free men without lawful judgement. It did nothing about voting or serfdom; England kept its monarchy.

questions.stem: Magna Carta is now seen as a foundation of modern rights, yet in 1215 who mainly benefited from it?
options: Serfs, who were freed from working on their lord's land
Every adult, who gained the right to elect a parliament
The king, whose power over the barons was increased
The barons and other free men, especially the powerful
questions.explanation: Magna Carta protected 'free men', and most people at the time were unfree villeins, so its benefits went mainly to barons, the Church and other free landholders. Its later importance came as later generations reinterpreted it as a guarantee of due process and the rule of law for everyone, influencing documents such as the United States Constitution.

questions.stem: What was trial by ordeal?
options: A hearing in which twelve local men decided guilt after listening carefully to the evidence
A punishment in which an offender was locked in the stocks for public mockery
A fine paid to the victim's family, set according to the victim's rank
A painful test, such as carrying hot iron, believed to reveal God's judgement
questions.explanation: In an ordeal the accused might carry red-hot iron or be lowered into water, and the result was taken as a sign from God of guilt or innocence. A hearing by twelve local men is an early jury, which gradually replaced ordeals after the Church withdrew its support for them in 1215.

questions.stem: Which medieval punishment locked an offender's feet in a wooden frame in a public place so that people could mock them?
options: The ducking stool
Trial by combat
Excommunication
The stocks
questions.explanation: The stocks held an offender's ankles in holes in a wooden board, often in the village square, for petty crimes such as drunkenness. A ducking stool was a chair on a long beam used to plunge someone into water, a different public punishment.

questions.stem: What was the main aim of the First Crusade, called by Pope Urban II in 1095?
options: To convert the pagan Vikings of Scandinavia to Christianity
To defend the city of Rome from a Mongol invasion
To drive the English armies out of northern France
To capture Jerusalem and the Holy Land from Muslim rule
questions.explanation: Urban II answered a request for help from the Byzantine emperor and urged Christians to take Jerusalem, which crusaders captured in 1099. The Mongols did not reach Europe until the 1200s, so they could not have been the target in 1095.

questions.stem: Which Muslim leader recaptured Jerusalem from the crusaders in 1187?
options: Saladin
Muhammad
Genghis Khan
Suleiman the Magnificent
questions.explanation: Saladin, Sultan of Egypt and Syria, defeated the crusader army at Hattin in 1187 and then took Jerusalem; his success led to the Third Crusade under Richard the Lionheart. Suleiman the Magnificent was an Ottoman sultan of the 1500s, centuries later.

questions.stem: Which long-term effect of the Crusades on Europe do many historians point to?
options: Lasting Christian rule over Jerusalem and the rest of the Holy Land
The end of feudalism across Europe within a few years of 1099
Lasting trust and friendship between Christians and Muslims
Growing trade with the eastern Mediterranean, enriching Venice and Genoa
questions.explanation: Crusader states and the ships that supplied them strengthened trade links with the eastern Mediterranean, bringing goods such as spices, silk and sugar and enriching Italian trading cities. Christian rule over Jerusalem was short — the city was lost in 1187 — and the violence of the Crusades left bitterness on both sides.

questions.stem: What was a guild in a medieval town?
options: An association of merchants or craftsmen that set prices and standards
A tall wooden wall built around a town to defend its people from attack
A Church court that put suspected heretics on trial
A strip of land that serfs farmed for the lord of the manor
questions.explanation: Guilds controlled a trade in a town: they set prices and quality, trained apprentices and looked after members and their families in hard times. Church courts were a separate system run by bishops, not by merchants or craftsmen.

questions.stem: Why did many medieval towns seek a charter from the king or a lord?
options: It let the local bishop appoint the town's mayor and council
It granted rights such as holding markets and running their own affairs
It released the townspeople from paying any royal taxes for ever
It allowed the town to raise its own army against the king
questions.explanation: A charter was a written grant of rights — to hold markets and fairs, collect tolls, run local courts and choose officials — usually bought from the king or lord. Towns still paid taxes and dues; the charter often set a fixed sum instead of many separate charges.

questions.stem: The Islamic calendar begins with the Hijra in 622 CE. What was the Hijra?
options: The building of the Dome of the Rock
Muhammad's journey from Mecca to Medina
The crusaders' capture of Jerusalem
The birth of Muhammad in the city of Mecca
questions.explanation: In 622 Muhammad and his followers left Mecca for Medina, where he set up the first Muslim community; year 1 of the Islamic calendar starts there. Muhammad was born around 570, about fifty years earlier, so his birth is not the starting point.

questions.stem: By the early 700s, Muslim armies had expanded the caliphate into which part of Europe?
options: Denmark and the southern part of Scandinavia
Northern Germany and the coast of the Baltic Sea
Most of the Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal)
Southern England and the east coast of Ireland
questions.explanation: Muslim forces crossed from North Africa into Iberia in 711 and within a few years ruled most of it, which they called al-Andalus; Córdoba became one of Europe's greatest cities. Muslim rule never reached Britain or Scandinavia.

questions.stem: What is a caliphate?
options: A Muslim state ruled by a caliph, seen as successor to Muhammad
A Christian state ruled directly by the pope and his cardinals from Rome
A trade route linking China with the Mediterranean Sea
A Muslim place of worship topped with a tall minaret
questions.explanation: A caliph was regarded as the successor to Muhammad as leader of the Muslim community, and the lands he ruled formed a caliphate, such as the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates. A Muslim place of worship is a mosque.

questions.stem: What were the Silk Roads?
options: A network of trade routes linking China, Central Asia and the Mediterranean
A single paved highway built by the Romans to connect the city of Rome and China
A chain of sea ports that linked Europe with the Americas
A set of roads inside China used only for carrying silk
questions.explanation: The Silk Roads were many overland routes (with sea routes across the Indian Ocean) along which silk, spices, paper and ideas moved between East Asia, the Middle East and Europe. They carried far more than silk and were never one built road.

questions.stem: How did Muslim scholars in cities such as Baghdad and Córdoba influence learning in medieval Europe?
options: By closing their libraries to all Christian and Jewish scholars
By preserving and building on Greek works later translated into Latin
By introducing Roman numerals, which Europeans had never used before
By inventing movable-type printing and teaching it to European monks
questions.explanation: Scholars in the Islamic world translated and expanded Greek works on philosophy, medicine and mathematics; in the 1100s many were translated from Arabic into Latin in places like Toledo. Arabic scholarship brought Europe the Hindu–Arabic numerals, including zero — Roman numerals were Europe's own older system.

questions.stem: Gothic cathedrals such as Notre-Dame de Paris are known for which features?
options: Onion-shaped domes, minarets and walls covered in mosaics
Pointed arches, flying buttresses and large stained-glass windows
Rounded arches, very thick walls and small, narrow windows
Flat concrete roofs, steel girders and huge walls of plate-glass windows
questions.explanation: Gothic builders used pointed arches and flying buttresses to carry the weight of tall walls outward, which made room for huge stained-glass windows. Rounded arches, thick walls and small windows describe the earlier Romanesque style.

questions.stem: Which path in life allowed some medieval women to gain an education and live outside marriage?
options: Being ordained a priest
Studying at a university
Joining a convent as a nun
Training as a knight
questions.explanation: Convents taught many nuns to read and write, and abbesses such as Hildegard of Bingen became writers, composers and leaders. Medieval universities and the priesthood were open only to men.

questions.stem: In 1517 Martin Luther began the Reformation. What did it lead to?
options: The reuniting of the Catholic and Orthodox churches
The end of Christianity across northern Europe
The pope moving the papacy from Rome to Paris
Protestant churches separate from the Catholic Church
questions.explanation: Luther's criticism of the Church, beginning with the sale of indulgences, split Western Christianity: Protestant churches formed, especially in northern Europe, separate from the Catholic Church led by the pope. Northern Europe remained Christian — it became largely Protestant rather than giving up Christianity.

questions.stem: Why do historians treat King Arthur as a figure of legend rather than a proven historical king?
options: No reliable record written in his supposed lifetime mentions him
His grave was opened and shown to belong to a Roman general
Every record of his reign was destroyed by the invading Normans in 1066
He is known to have been invented by William Shakespeare
questions.explanation: Arthur is supposed to have lived around 500 CE, but the first mentions of him come centuries later, and the famous stories of Camelot and the Round Table were written later still, from the 1100s. Without evidence close to the time, historians cannot confirm he existed. Shakespeare wrote around 1600, long after the Arthur legends were well known.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the claim that religion was the main source of knowledge and authority in medieval Europe?
options: Scientists tested every claim by experiment, whatever the Church said
Nearly all scholars were clergy, and the Church ran most schools
Most peasants read the Bible for themselves in their own language
Kings in every European country were elected by the people
questions.explanation: Education, book-making and scholarship were largely in the hands of priests, monks and nuns, and universities taught theology as the highest subject, so the Church shaped what people learned and believed. Most peasants could not read at all, and the Bible was usually in Latin.

questions.stem: In which years did the Black Death sweep through Europe?
questions.explanation: The Black Death reached Sicily in 1347 and spread across Europe until about 1351. The other dates belong to the Norman Conquest, the start of the Reformation and the First World War.

questions.stem: Ancient DNA from victims' skeletons shows that the Black Death was caused by:
options: smallpox, from a virus spread by coughing
cholera, from drinking polluted river water
malaria, spread by the bites of mosquitoes
plague, from the bacterium Yersinia pestis
questions.explanation: Scientists have found Yersinia pestis DNA in Black Death burial pits, confirming it was plague, usually spread by fleas living on rats; the pneumonic form could also spread from person to person through coughing. Cholera and malaria are different diseases with different causes.

questions.stem: How did the Black Death reach Europe?
options: With crusaders returning home to France from Jerusalem after the First Crusade
On Viking longships returning from Greenland and North America
With sailors returning to Spain from voyages to the Americas
Along trade routes from Asia, then on ships from the Black Sea to Italy
questions.explanation: The plague spread from Central Asia along the Silk Roads to the Black Sea port of Caffa, and Genoese ships carried it to Messina in Sicily in 1347, then on to other Mediterranean ports. The First Crusade ended in 1099, about 250 years before the outbreak.

questions.stem: Roughly what share of Europe's population died in the Black Death?
options: About nine people in every ten
Between about one-third and one-half
About one person in every hundred
About one person in every ten
questions.explanation: Historians estimate that between a third and a half of Europe's people died, though the exact figure is debated because records are incomplete. One in ten is far too low: whole villages were emptied, and cities such as Florence lost more than half their people.

questions.stem: Which explanation for the Black Death did many people give at the time?
options: It was a punishment sent by God for people's sins
It was caused by bacteria carried in rats' fleas
It was spread by germs left on unwashed hands
It was caught by drinking milk from sick cows
questions.explanation: Most people believed the plague was God's punishment, while doctors also blamed 'miasma' (poisoned air) and the alignment of the planets. Bacteria and germs were not discovered until the 1800s, so no one at the time could have explained it that way, even though that is the real cause.

questions.stem: Who were the flagellants during the Black Death?
options: Peasants who marched on London to demand lower taxes
Groups who whipped themselves in public to show repentance to God
Doctors who wore beaked masks while treating plague victims
Officials who kept ships waiting offshore before they landed
questions.explanation: Flagellants travelled from town to town whipping themselves, hoping that their suffering would persuade God to end the plague; the pope condemned the movement in 1349. Beaked plague-doctor costumes date from the 1600s, long after the Black Death.

questions.stem: Ships arriving in Venice and Ragusa (Dubrovnik) from plague areas had to wait offshore before anyone could land. Which modern word comes from this practice?
options: Vaccination
Hospital
Epidemic
Quarantine
questions.explanation: The waiting period was later set at forty days — quaranta giorni in Italian — which gave us the word quarantine. Vaccination was developed by Edward Jenner in the 1790s, centuries after the Black Death.

questions.stem: Medieval doctors often treated the plague by bleeding patients. Which idea was this based on?
options: Fresh blood from a donor could replace the patient's own blood
Losing blood would drive the fleas out of the patient's body
The body had four humours that had to be kept in balance
Germs in the blood had to be drained before they multiplied
questions.explanation: Following ancient Greek medicine, doctors believed health depended on balancing four humours — blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile — so they drained blood to restore balance. Germs were unknown until the 1800s, so no medieval doctor thought in those terms.

questions.stem: Why were Jewish communities attacked in many parts of Europe during the Black Death?
options: They were found to have carried the plague into Europe from Asia
They had been ordered by the pope to leave Europe before 1347
They were known to have refused to care for plague victims
They were falsely accused of poisoning wells to spread the plague
questions.explanation: Frightened people looked for someone to blame, and Jewish communities were falsely accused of poisoning wells; thousands were murdered, for example in Strasbourg in 1349. Pope Clement VI pointed out that Jewish people were dying of the plague too and condemned the attacks, so the Church had not ordered them out.

questions.stem: Which Italian writer described the plague in Florence at the start of his book The Decameron?
options: Giovanni Boccaccio
Niccolò Machiavelli
Dante Alighieri
Marco Polo
questions.explanation: Boccaccio lived through the plague in Florence in 1348 and opened The Decameron with a vivid description of it. Dante died in 1321, before the Black Death, and Machiavelli lived more than a century later.

questions.stem: Why did wages for labourers in England rise after the Black Death?
options: The king ordered that all wages had to be doubled
The Church began paying wages to every peasant
New farm machines made each worker more productive
So many workers had died that labour was scarce
questions.explanation: With perhaps a third or more of workers dead, surviving labourers could demand higher pay or move to lords who offered more. The king actually tried to stop wages rising, through the Statute of Labourers in 1351.

questions.stem: The Statute of Labourers (1351) tried to hold wages at their level before the plague. What does this law suggest?
options: The plague had left too many workers for the jobs available
Prices had fallen so far that higher wages were not needed
Landowners feared losing control as surviving workers demanded more
Peasants had asked the king to keep their wages low, steady and fair
questions.explanation: A law forcing wages down only makes sense if wages were rising, so the statute shows landowners struggling to keep workers on the old terms. Labour was scarce, not plentiful, which is exactly why workers could ask for more.

questions.stem: Which grievance helped spark the Peasants' Revolt in England in 1381?
options: A ban on peasants attending church services
The arrival of the first books printed in English
A new poll tax charged on almost every adult
The closing of the monasteries by the king
questions.explanation: The third poll tax in four years, together with anger at laws holding down wages, led peasants led by Wat Tyler to march on London. The monasteries were closed by Henry VIII in the 1530s, and printing came to England in the 1470s.

questions.stem: Why do historians say the Black Death should not be studied as only a European event?
options: It also killed vast numbers in Asia, the Middle East and North Africa
It began in England before spreading to the rest of the world
Its European records have all been lost or destroyed
It was recorded only by Asian writers, never by Europeans
questions.explanation: The plague killed huge numbers in cities such as Cairo and Damascus, and the North African historian Ibn Khaldun, who lost his parents to it, wrote about how it devastated the Islamic world. It reached Europe from Asia, not the other way round, and European writers such as Boccaccio recorded it too.
